My family has farmed this land in Quzhou for three generations. I know this soil, I know this weather. At 76, my back isn't what it was — my son helps when he visits from the city, and I hire the village machine cooperative for plowing and seeding. I'm not going to try anything clever. I grow what I've always grown, what this land and this county are known for: winter wheat and summer corn.

I have 8 mu of contracted land. Last autumn I planted wheat on all of it, as I do every year. Now it's spring, the wheat is in the jointing stage. After I harvest it in June, I'll turn around immediately and plant corn on the same fields — the rotation we've done here for decades. This is the safest path. Both crops have government purchase prices, both I can sell to the grain station in town without worrying about finding a buyer.

I'll use the improved wheat seed I bought from the township supply store — same variety I used last year, it performed well. For corn I always use hybrid seed, everyone here does, the yields are much better than the old varieties my father used.

I apply fertilizer the way I learned: base fertilizer before seeding, then top-dress the wheat in spring. My amounts haven't changed much in years. I irrigate wheat three times — the winter water to protect roots from freezing, jointing water, and grain-filling water. We draw from the well using the village irrigation group. Corn gets natural summer rainfall mostly, just one extra irrigation if August is dry.

I don't over-apply pesticide — it's expensive — but I spray the wheat for aphids and rust, and treat the corn for armyworm if needed.
